findings.title: Unprotected GET requests change notification preferences
findings.description:
Both new GET routes invoke `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, which immediately saves changes using the logged-in user's session. Rails' CSRF protection does not protect GET requests, and this action explicitly bypasses `check_xhr`. An attacker can therefore direct a logged-in browser to a predictable topic URL and change its notification settings without authorization from the user.

Make GET display the unsubscribe page and perform the change through a CSRF-protected POST, or use a securely scoped unsubscribe token rather than relying solely on session cookies.

findings.title: Missing topic-user records cause an unsubscribe error
findings.description:
`TopicUser.find_by` can return `nil`, but the next statement unconditionally calls `notification_level`. Inspecting `TopicView` confirms that constructing a topic view does not create this record. A logged-in user following a forwarded unsubscribe link for a topic they have not visited can consequently receive a server error.

Handle an absent record and create the required muted preference, preferably through the existing `TopicUser.change` mechanism.

findings.title: Direct saves allow automatic tracking to undo an unsubscribe
findings.description:
The endpoint changes `notification_level` directly without setting `notifications_reason_id` or `notifications_changed_at`. In contrast, `TopicUser.change` records an explicit `user_changed` reason and publishes the notification-level change.

This omission affects behavior: `TopicUser.update_last_read` automatically promotes topics to tracking when `notifications_reason_id` is null and the reading-time threshold is exceeded. For an automatically tracked topic, unsubscribing leaves that reason null, so subsequent reading can undo the user's choice. Use the established notification-change API so explicit unsubscribe decisions remain persistent and are propagated consistently.
